transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-07-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording linked)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood Product), Priya (Helio CTO), Liam (Helio ML Eng), Sofia (Helio Infra), Arman (Helio SRE)

Summary:
Quick demo/walkthrough of the model catalog filter + bench slicing features in Console and the API. Focus on how to choose open models for different workload slices (short-form customer chat vs. long multi-turn summarization), and discussion of deployability matrix across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem). We covered bench methodology, cost/latency tradeoffs, and Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching, quant profiles). Agreed next steps and deliverables.

Topics covered:
- Catalog filters and scoring (slicing by input distribution)
- Bench slicing: per-workload measurement and guardrails
- Compatibility matrix: kernel/quantization/deployability fields
- API vs Console flow for evaluation and pilot
- Private deploy considerations: KMS, audit logs, network egress
- Redwood Optimize suggestions for cost/latency

Action items (short list):
- Maya: send benchmark template + cost model
- Diego: run a small KV-cache demo and doc snippets
- Priya: share sample prompt sets and SLA targets

Transcript (timestamps approximate, auto-transcribed, some errors):
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm Maya, i'm the AE on the Helio account, i'll hand over to Diego for the deep demo but first high level?
[00:14] Priya: hey, thanks, yes, from Helio — our team wants to understand how to pick open models from Redwood's catalog based on our workloads; we have low-latency chat on edge nodes and heavy doc summarization in batch.
[00:30] Diego: great, that's exactly what the catalog-slicing feature is for. i'll share my screen — console.redwood.io, go to Catalog > Picklist. you can set filters by tokens, by seq length distribution, by architecture, and we surface a deployability score.
[01:02] Liam: quick q — what do you mean by deployability score? is that like whether it can run on fp16 on A100 vs quantized on T4?
[01:11] Diego: yeah, it's a composite. under the hood it looks at kernel readiness, quantization friendliness, memory footprint, and known perf on our Dedicated fleets. it then shows compatibility for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. sometimes the product name is Redwood Dedicate in the UI — small typo in the label, ha.
[01:36] Sofia: and does that include our private on-prem images? we have air-gapped clusters so encryption/KMS is critical.
[01:42] Evan: quick note — Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. Diego, maybe show the private checklist?
[01:50] Diego: sure, toggling to the private column; we also annotate models with expected fallback variants — e.g., if a 16-bit float kernel isn't available, there's a quantized 4-bit fallback. the matrix shows perf deltas.

[02:14] Diego (screen): i want to highlight bench slicing: instead of a single benchmark you upload workload slices. here's an example: slice A = short chat (average 32 tokens), slice B = multi-turn summary (avg 1200 tokens truncated but with long context), slice C = embeddings heavy. for each slice we run latency p50/p95, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens.
[02:46] Priya: so we can see p95 for only the multi-turn slice, not conflated with the short chat numbers? good.
[02:53] Diego: exactly. that lets you pick a model for each route in our API — you can route by path /chat -> model X, /summaries -> model Y. the routing policy can prefer lower cost at some times and fall back to higher quality when latency SLO is met.

[03:20] Liam: curious about the bench methodology — how reproducible is it? do you run on the same GPU families? what about batching?
[03:28] Diego: we try to be consistent. bench runner uses standardized concurrency and sequence length distributions you provide. we run on fleet-representative hardware, and we surface the kernel compile flags and quant profile. for customer pilots we can run the same bench on Dedicated or on a private node when possible so numbers are apples-to-apples.
[03:52] Arman: and network egress adds variability. can we pin tests to our VPC region?
[03:58] Maya: yes, for Private we run in your VPC region; for Dedicated we have region affinity options. we'll note that in the follow-up.

[05:00] (15s of static, then Diego continues)
[05:15] Diego: demo — filtering by "low latency" and token length. pick two candidate open models — an LlaMa-2-like 13B (auto-labeled) and a quant-optimized 7B variant. the compatibility matrix shows the 13B compiles well on A100, but on T4 it needs a 4-bit quant fallback with 9-12% perf delta. the 7B quant optimized has better cost but shows a slight drop on multi-turn coherence.
[05:48] Priya: hmm, we care more about convo coherence for chat, but cost matters at scale. can Redwood Optimize give a suggestion?
[05:55] Evan: yes, Optimize synthesizes historical traffic, suggests batching windows, prefix caching and quant profiles. it will recommend a conservative quant (e.g., q4_0) for chat and q3a for batch summarization where throughput dominates.

[07:20] (Speaker label glitch: "Speaker 2" shows instead of Liam)
[07:25] Speaker 2: are the quant recommendations model-specific or workload-specific?
[07:30] Diego: both. we score model x with q4 and q3a on that workload slice and show expected quality delta (we put a small eval set to measure regression). you'll see a quality vs cost chart.

[09:00] Priya: will you run evals on our prompt set? we were worried about hallucination in summarization.
[09:07] Maya: yes, that's part of the pilot scope — Helio provides prompts, we run benchmarks + quality evals and produce regression alerts.

[10:15] Diego: switching to API usage — you can call Redwood's /v1/generate and set route id that maps to a specific model for that path. here's the example we use in the docs (some chars may be munged in the transcript): POST /v1/generate {"route":"/chat","model":"redwood://catalog/model-13b-q4" , "stream":true }
[10:50] Liam: what about KV cache priming — we preload context for multi-turn in edge nodes?
[10:55] Diego: yes, we expose KV cache APIs; we recommend prefix caching for repeated system instructions and a short-lived sticky cache for session context. i'll attach the runbook that explains cache TTLs and warm-up.

[12:45] (brief crosstalk, someone mutes/unmutes)
[13:10] Diego: i want to show the bench details page — here the runner logs compile-time kernel choices, sequence length histogram, concurrency setting, and the raw token timing trace. the console has a CSV export if you want to ingest into your internal cost model.
[13:45] Arman: on Private, how do we handle model artifacts? do you push containers to our registry or do we pull?
[13:52] Evan: two options: we can push signed artifacts into your registry (requires registry access) or we provide an on-prem bundle you install which pulls via an internal fetcher. both support air-gap transfer via signed tarball.
[14:20] Sofia: for compliance, we need audit logs and token-level usage. can we get per-token attribution?
[14:27] Maya: yes, Private includes audit logs and per-route cost/latency breakdowns. we also support customer-managed KMS for key encryption.

[16:00] Diego: circling back to the compatibility matrix — note that some models in the open roster have limited kernel support. you'll see "partial" flags where only attention kernels are optimized but KV cache path is pending. those often require a compile pass or kernel mapping on Private.
[16:25] Priya: if a model is marked partial, how long to production-ready on Private?
[16:30] Diego: depends. small kernels can be shipped within 2-4 weeks with our compile team; bigger architectural gaps take longer. for pilots we recommend picking 1-2 models with full compatibility and 1 fallback for quality checks.

[18:05] Liam: can Redwood help with quantization? we don't have in-house quant experts.
[18:12] Evan: yes, Optimize includes quant profile suggestions and we've shipped a "quant-health" report that shows expected quality penalties and fallback policy. Diego: we usually recommend conservative quant for customer-facing chat.

[20:00] (screen: routing policies)
[20:10] Diego: last part — routing: you can set policy by latency threshold, cost budget, or region. example: route /chat requests in EU to model-eu-13b, but if p95 exceeds 600ms swap to smaller 7B variant. policies can be tested in a canary rollout.
[20:34] Priya: if we do canary, can we get automatic fallback to Hosted if Dedicated hits capacity?
[20:40] Diego: yes, our smart routing supports fallback tiers — Dedicated -> Hosted -> Compatible quant-fallback. note that data residency rules may prevent cross-region fallback.

[22:00] (customer asks about benchmarking reproducibility; Diego opens a note)
[22:15] Diego: pro-tip: when you upload sample prompts, include expected token distribution. Optimize can then suggest a batched concurrency and kernel selection that minimize p95.

[24:30] Priya: ok show us a specific example for our chat traffic — what do you recommend today given our brief?
[24:40] Diego: quick take: for chat (low-latency 50-150ms target p50, p95 < 400ms): go with the quant-optimized 7B on our Dedicated fleet in EU region, use q4_0, and enable prefix caching. for long summaries (throughput-focused), use the 13B with q3a on Dedicated or Private with batch windows and a higher latency SLO.
[25:12] Liam: and cost differences?
[25:16] Diego: ballpark — 7B q4 route: $X per 1k tokens (cheaper), 13B q3a: about 2.5x cost but better ROUGE/QA on the eval set. we'll put exact numbers in the follow-up sheet.

[26:50] (brief silence, someone types in chat)
[27:05] Priya: security question: do you support SSO/SAML + RBAC for access to logs?
[27:12] Maya: yes SSO/SAML and role-based access control are supported for Console and Private control plane.

[28:30] (Diego shows a small KV demo)
[29:05] Diego: i executed an example where session keys are primed; you can see the p50/p95 drop after warm-up. note: transcribed sample below may cut punctuation.

[31:15] Priya: one concern — some of the open models have unknown license or export-control constraints. does Redwood flag licensing issues?
[31:23] Evan: we annotate models with license tags and a basic policy note; for anything ambiguous our onboarding will do a legal check.

[33:40] Liam: how long does a pilot typically take? we'd like to measure both perf and quality.
[33:48] Maya: pilot is usually 3-6 weeks: week 1 onboarding and prompt set prep, weeks 2-3 bench runs and evals, week 4 consolidation and recommendations. timeline flexible.

[35:00] (customer asks about competitors)
[35:05] Priya: are there cases where OpenAI or HF infra would be better?
[35:11] Maya: sometimes when you need a proprietary model or zero-admin access, other vendors win on simplicity. Redwood's strength is unified serving across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private with observability and cost controls.

[37:20] Diego: another demo snippet — Optimize runbook suggestions for batching: use micro-batches for chat (to keep p95 low) and larger batches for summarization. show recommended concurrency 8-12 for a single GPU slice on 13B.

[38:40] Sofia: for Private, what's the upgrade story for runtime and kernels?
[38:46] Evan: we ship kernel updates as signed packages; you can schedule maintenance windows. for air-gapped, we provide signed binaries and a checklist.

[41:00] (15s pause, then Q&A)
[41:20] Priya: what do you need from our side to start a pilot?
[41:27] Maya: three things — sample prompts, target SLAs and traffic profile, and a contact for infra access if Private.

[42:05] Priya: we'll share that by Monday.
[42:08] Maya: great, we'll follow up with an initial SOW and pilot plan.

[44:00] (closing recap)
[44:10] Maya: recap — Maya will send benchmark template and cost model; Diego will prepare KV cache priming runbook; Evan will include quant profile suggestions from Optimize. Helio will share prompt sets and SLA targets. next meeting: technical deep-dive if Helio chooses Private, target week of 2028-07-16.

[46:50] (informal chatter, small jokes; someone says "thanks everyone")
[47:05] Priya: thanks all, that was very helpful.
[47:10] Liam: appreciate it.
[47:12] Maya: thanks, bye.
[47:15] (recording stopped)

Notes on transcript quality: speaker attribution occasionally generic and some proper nouns mis-transcribed (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate"), timestamps approximate.
